gens.text:
The theatre lies two floors below the street, a long white room whose ceiling carries a single articulated lamp on a steel arm, and because the glass of the observation gallery has been darkened for the morning the room holds no weather and the hour is unguessable from inside it, and the team assembles beneath the lamp in the order their hands will be wanted, the scrub nurse first at the instrument table she has laid out in four ranks, to count by touch the clamps and the sponges and the fine curved needles that she will pass without looking up, and she speaks each number aloud as she goes, so that the circulating nurse, writing at the wall, can match her tally before the drapes go down, until the two columns agree and nothing is unaccounted for.

The patient lies already asleep on the table, a woman of sixty-one who was walked through this room yesterday at her own request, who now shows nothing above the drape but the shaved and painted field of her upper abdomen, whose breathing has been handed over to a machine that sighs in a rhythm slower than anyone's in the room; the anaesthetist sits at her head behind a low green screen, where the monitors stack their four colours, where the pressure cuff inflates every three minutes, where a strip of tape holds the tube at the corner of her mouth.

The surgeon arrives with her hands raised and dripping at the level of her collarbone and turns her back to the door to be gowned; the nurse ties her at the neck and the waist, then holds each glove open like a mouth until the fingers are in.

The field is painted a second time with a sponge stick that sweeps outward in flattening spirals from the midline, and no stroke returns toward the centre; then the drapes are laid, first the two side towels, then the fenestrated sheet whose window frames a rectangle of stained skin and nothing else.

The surgeon asks for the blade, which the nurse sets into her palm handle first and announces by name, and she lays the flat of her left hand on the skin to stretch it taut before she cuts; the first incision runs eight inches below the ribs, a single unhurried stroke that opens the dermis to the yellow layer beneath.

The bleeding that follows is small and orderly, little beads along the line which the assistant takes in turn with the forceps, and the diathermy answers each with a tick and a thread of smoke that the suction catches at once, and the knife goes deeper now through the sheath and the muscle is separated along its fibres rather than cut, and the peritoneum is lifted in two pairs of forceps, tented away from whatever lies under it, and opened between them with scissors, so the first breath of the cavity escapes and the smell of warm tissue reaches the mask.

The retractor is brought in and spread by degrees to hold the edges apart, and its arms are locked to the frame at the table's rail.

Moist packs are placed to hold the bowel aside; the assistant's hand steadies them; the lamp is swung an inch and refocused, and the head of it is wiped; the surgeon puts two fingers into the wound and reads the organ by feel before she looks at it.

The mass is where the scan said it would be, high on the greater curve; she frees it along the bloodless plane with a blunt dissector and takes the feeding vessels one at a time, clipping each twice on the side that stays and once on the side that goes, and dividing between.

The specimen comes away whole into a steel bowl, and the bowl is lifted from the field; the nurse labels it and signs the label and carries it to the door, where a porter waits with the cold box and takes it without entering; the surgeon irrigates with warm saline until the fluid returns clear, which the suction draws off in a falling note that thins as the cavity empties, and she waits while the assistant lifts each pack out in the order they went in, so that the count can be called aloud twice, to be answered twice from the wall, before anything is closed.

The nurse reports the figures correct, a tally that matches the one taken before the first cut.

The closure proceeds in layers from the depth outward, a slow reversal of everything done, and because the muscle must hold against a cough the surgeon runs a heavy looped suture through the sheath in wide bites and ties it against the knot she buried at the far end, after she has tested the line with a finger that finds no gap, and the skin is brought together with a subcuticular stitch that leaves no marks on either side; a flat dressing is pressed down, the drapes are peeled back, the lamp is switched off.

The theatre opens at a quarter past seven with a light that has no source anyone can point to, a flat white that falls from the dome and refuses to make shadows, and because the room must be colder than comfort allows, the vents breathe steadily along the baseboards and the gowned bodies acquire a faint stiffness at the shoulders; the scrub nurse, who has counted her instruments twice already, begins to count them a third time, laying each clamp in its ordained furrow of green cloth so that nothing will be missing at the end, when the cavity is closed and the tally must be read aloud to satisfy the room, and the circulating nurse records the number.

The patient lies under drapes that leave only a rectangle of abdomen exposed, a rectangle painted amber with antiseptic, a field that the surgeon studies for several seconds before consenting to touch it; the anaesthetist speaks from behind the screen, since her monitors are steady, since the pressure has settled at ninety over sixty, since the agent has reached the depth she wants.

The surgeon asks for the blade and receives it handle first, the nurse's palm flat as a dish; nobody says anything further, because the next minute belongs entirely to the hand.

The first incision runs eleven centimetres along a line that the marker pen laid down an hour ago; the skin parts without protest, and under it the yellow fat opens like something that had been waiting to be allowed.

Diathermy follows, a thin pen that hisses where it meets the bleeding margin and lifts a grey thread of smoke, sealing the small vessels before they can assert themselves; the suction catheter takes the smoke away, and the assistant holds the retractor that keeps the wound honest, its blades set wide enough to admit two hands.

Beneath the fat lies the sheath, a tough white membrane that the surgeon nicks to begin it and then opens with scissors, a membrane whose fibres run crosswise to the cut; the muscle below is not divided but separated, pushed apart along its grain by two fingers that work slowly, fingers that know the peritoneum is thin here and that feel for the bowel beneath, lifting the glistening layer in forceps and tenting it upward to be certain nothing is caught, for the alternative is an injury discovered too late, and the surgeon has seen that once.

The peritoneum opens, letting a sigh of warm air out of the body, and the inside of the patient becomes a landscape under the lamp.

The assistant packs the loops away with moist gauze; the count is noted; the surgeon reaches past the omentum and finds what she came for, the inflamed appendage swollen to the thickness of a thumb, and she lifts it clear of the pelvis before dividing anything.

The mesentery is taken first: the clips go on in a line, and the vessels are cut between them while the base is crushed with a clamp, tied with absorbable thread, tied again a centimetre lower, and finally transected with a clean knife.

The specimen goes into a pot that the circulating nurse labels and seals: the stump is buried with a purse-string, and the cavity is irrigated with warm saline that comes out cloudy at first and then clear. The team now reverses itself: the gauze is withdrawn and counted against the board, the retractor is loosened by the assistant, who waits until the muscle has slid back over the peritoneum, allowing the planes to settle as they were before the knife came down.

The closure proceeds upward through the layers that the opening came down through.

The sheath takes a running suture of looped nylon, and when the last throw is laid the surgeon tests it with a finger, since a weak repair becomes a hernia in a year, since the thread must bear the cough that is coming in the recovery bay; the skin is approximated with staples that click twice each, and a dressing is pressed down over the line. The count is correct, the anaesthetist begins to lighten her, and the theatre reverts to its ordinary noise.

The theatre waits under a bank of lamps that have been angled by the circulating nurse an hour before, and when the patient is wheeled through the double doors the anaesthetist counts the breaths aloud, the registrar checks the consent band against the board; the surgeon steps to the right of the table, where the drapes have already been squared to the iliac crest, and asks for the blade, which the scrub nurse lifts from the Mayo tray and lays handle-first into the open palm, because nothing is permitted to travel point-forward across a sterile field, so that the count may stay honest from the first minute, when the instruments, laid in rows, are told over twice and signed for in the ledger.

The first incision is a single unhurried stroke below the costal margin, which parts the skin in a line the width of four fingers, which weeps along its whole length almost at once, which the assistant is ready to blot with a folded swab; the diathermy answers in a thin blue note, the smell of it rises as the extractor labours, the hand does not pause while the fat is divided, and the fascia shows white beneath.

The surgeon names each layer as it is opened — the tone is flat, deliberately uninflected — because the trainee on the far side of the drapes is learning the order in which a body consents to be entered.

Beneath the fascia lies the rectus sheath, which is scored transversely and peeled back; the muscle fibres are separated by blunt finger, not cut, a manoeuvre that spares the segmental nerves running within them.

A retractor is placed and racked open two clicks at a time, a frame that the assistant steadies with both hands and does not release, the surgeon pausing to let the tissue accommodate before the third click is taken; the peritoneum tents under the forceps, a glossy membrane that two pairs of toothed grips must lift clear of the bowel.

The cavity is opened with a short snip of the scissors, a cut made deliberately small so as to admit the finger first, which sweeps for adhesions and finds none, and the opening is then extended along the length of the wound with the blades riding on that guiding finger, which keeps the bowel down, which keeps the bladder below the pubic line; warm packs are laid to the left, warm packs are laid to the right, and the lamp is swung a hand's breadth to bring the field into true light, since the shadow of the surgeon's own wrist had been falling across the duodenum and the assistant could not see the clamp.

The gallbladder is delivered into view, the fundus grasped to put the cystic pedicle on stretch, and the peritoneum over it is teased away with a swab on a stick.

The dissection proceeds slowly here, the object being to see two structures and two only — the window is made, the lymph node is lifted off the artery and set aside, and the cystic duct is encircled with a right-angled forceps before any clip is loaded.

The surgeon declares the critical view aloud; the assistant confirms it, the anaesthetist notes the pressure holding steady, and the clips are applied in turn — two proximal, one distal — while the hook divides between them and the stump retracts a little and sits quiet.

The gallbladder is lifted from its bed in short strokes of the hook, the plane kept close to the liver, the bed inspected afterward for the small weeping vessels that are touched with the coagulator and blanch; the specimen goes into a bag, which the circulating nurse receives at the edge of the table, which she labels and carries to the bench while the scrub nurse begins the count again, calling the swabs by tens, until the two tallies agree and the figure is written up.

The cavity is irrigated with warm saline and the fluid aspirated until it returns clear.

The closure runs upward in layers, a looped monofilament taking the sheath in continuous bites a centimetre from the edge and a centimetre apart, and when the knot is thrown the assistant holds the ends taut and the surgeon tests the line with a fingertip, feeling for the gap that a hurried stitch leaves; the skin is drawn together with subcuticular suture and dressed, the drapes that have shielded the field since the first minute come away in one sheet, and the patient is counted onto the trolley, the lamps dimmed, the theatre turned over for the next name on the board.

The theatre takes its light from a single articulated lamp overhead, which the circulating nurse angles until the field beneath it lies flat and shadowless, and because the patient has been draped to a rectangle of skin no wider than a hand, the room's attention narrows to that rectangle, a window of ochre-painted abdomen bordered by blue cloth, where the first mark is laid down in ink and the scalpel is brought up to begin, so that the surgeon, who has stood for a moment with the blade poised at a slight angle, settles her weight and draws it through the dermis in one unhurried stroke, pausing only where the line must curve to follow the rib margin, since a straight cut there would tent the tissue and leave a scar that puckers.

Beneath the dermis lies the fat, which parts dully and yellow, which bleeds in small insistent beads, which the assistant must blot and then seal with the diathermy tip; the pattern settles into rhythm — the forceps lift a vessel, the current hisses for half a second, the smoke is drawn off by the suction held steady at the wound's lip.

The fascia appears as a white sheet, glistening and tough; the surgeon nicks it with the blade, then opens it the length of the incision with scissors, while the assistant keeps the edges on tension.

Below the fascia the muscle is split rather than cut, fibres that separate along their own grain under two fingers, and the retractor is seated into the gap, whose blades are ratcheted open a notch at a time.

Now the peritoneum is lifted in two forceps, which the scrub nurse hands over without being asked, and the surgeon cuts between them to enter the cavity, after she has confirmed that no bowel is tented in the fold; the cavity breathes open, a cool slackening that the anaesthetist notes aloud before resuming his count.

Packs go in to shoulder the small intestine aside, soft wet gauze that the team counts audibly as it is placed, each one tailed with a radio-opaque strip, and the diseased segment is delivered into the wound, which has by now assumed the look of a shallow basin, which the lamp fills with a flat and even brightness, where the mesentery is fanned against the light, and the arcade of vessels is clamped in pairs and divided, the surgeon working from the gut wall outward to spare the blood supply of what remains, until the segment hangs on nothing, and the stapler is called for.

The jaws close twice to transect above and below the lesion, and the specimen is passed off the field in a basin.

The bowel ends are brought together to lie without tension, the lumens are checked, the stapler is fired across the common wall and the firing line inspected along its length, and the enterotomy is closed by hand because that join deserves a second opinion from the needle.

The irrigation comes next: two litres of warm saline are poured and suctioned back, and the surgeon watches the returning fluid until it runs clear of debris, the packs are withdrawn and counted against the board, the count is declared correct, and the retractor is unseated.

Closure proceeds in the reverse order of the opening: the peritoneum and fascia are taken as one layer, and a looped suture is run from each angle toward the middle, where the two sutures are tied to each other, and the knot is buried. Then the skin: a subcuticular line that the surgeon lays in short even bites, that she tightens only enough to appose the edges, so that the scar will fade to a pale thread, drawing the dermis level as she goes, while the assistant steadies the tissue with a toothed forceps.

A dressing is applied, which the nurse smooths from the centre outward.

The drapes come away, and the patient, who has not stirred, is uncovered to the warm air of the theatre while the anaesthetist lightens the gas and the monitors are read aloud one last time, each figure answered by the surgeon with a nod before she steps back from the table, and the team begins the business of the trolley and the doors, which open on the corridor light. The lamp is switched off.

The theatre lies under a ceiling of lamps whose hinged arms have been angled inward since the first count of instruments, and while the circulating nurse reads the patient's name aloud and the anaesthetist confirms the airway, the scrub nurse lifts the blade from its tray and sets it in the surgeon's palm, which closes on it without hurry, the hand being trained to wait for the moment the skin is taut, so that the first stroke travels cleanly through the prepared field, drawn from the costal margin downward in one continuous motion, the line opening behind the steel as a seam opens, and a thread of blood rising to meet it.

The assistant takes up the gauze that has been warmed for this purpose, which absorbs the first welling without smearing the margins, which the surgeon needs to see clearly in order to judge the depth already won; the diathermy pencil touches each small bleeder, a thin smoke lifts and is drawn away by the suction held near the wound, the vessels seal with a sound like a struck match, and the field grows pale again under the lamps.

Beneath the dermis the yellow fat parts easily, showing the glossy white of the anterior sheath; the surgeon nicks it, slides a finger beneath to lift it from the muscle, and the sheath divides along its fibres as the scissors travel.

The rectus muscle, which has lain compressed all morning under the drapes, is separated at the midline rather than cut; the retractor is set, and the blades are spread by the assistant, who holds them at the angle the surgeon indicates with two fingers.

The peritoneum rises as a grey tent between the forceps that the surgeon and the assistant hold opposed, and the knife is turned flat to open it without touching what lies beneath; a thin rush of fluid follows, which the suction takes before it can spill onto the drapes.

What the lamps now show is a loop of bowel, pale and faintly mobile, that the surgeon lifts to inspect its mesentery, which carries the arcade of vessels he has studied on the films; and the assistant packs the upper quadrant with moist swabs, which are counted aloud as they go in, and which the circulating nurse records on the board, so that nothing is left behind when the cavity is finally closed and the drapes come down.

The diseased segment is mobilised along its attachments, and the clamps are applied above and below the resection line.

The surgeon asks for the stapler, the nurse delivers it handle-first, the device is fired across the bowel, the staple line is inspected for bleeding, and the specimen is passed off the field as the pathologist's runner steps forward.

The anastomosis is begun at the mesenteric border: the stitches are placed at even intervals, and the knots are laid down flat so that the lumen stays open, the suture is drawn snug but never strangling, the needle is passed back to the nurse, and the junction is tested with gentle pressure.

Now the swabs come out one by one: the count is called and answered twice, the cavity is irrigated with warm saline until the returning fluid runs clear, which the assistant draws off with the sucker until the basin shows nothing but a faint tinge; and the surgeon runs a last hand along the gutters, feeling for the small slippery thing that no light reaches, which must be found before the first layer is laid, lest the count come short at the end and the whole closure be undone.

The peritoneum and the posterior sheath are taken in a single running layer that the assistant follows with the forceps.

The skin is closed with interrupted sutures, which the nurse cuts short at each knot, and when the last is tied the dressing is pressed flat and the drapes are peeled back in one movement, so that the patient reappears whole where a wound had been; the anaesthetist lightens the gas and speaks the patient's name, which draws a slow turn of the head; the instrument count is read a third time, the lamps are swung away, the theatre falls quiet.

The theatre lies two floors below the street, a white room whose air is kept three degrees cooler than the corridor outside, and because the lamps are already burning in their double arc the shadows have been driven out of the field entirely, and the only dark left is the dark under the drapes; the scrub nurse, who has counted her sponges twice, begins to lay out the instruments in the order they will be wanted, first the scalpel that waits nearest her right hand, then the retractors ranked behind it, so that when the surgeon asks she need not look down, and the asking itself may stay unhurried, as though nothing in the room were moving, while the clock on the far wall goes on dividing the hour.

The first incision is a line drawn just below the costal margin, a line the surgeon has already traced in sterile marker, a line she now opens with a single unhesitating draw, letting the blade travel at the speed her wrist has learned over twenty years; the skin parts, the fat beneath it stands open like a seam, and the assistant brings the suction forward before the first bright bead has time to gather.

Diathermy takes the small vessels one by one, their sealing audible as a series of short ticks under the hiss of the ventilator; the smell arrives, as it always does, half a second after the sound.

The fascia is next, a pale sheet that resists the knife longer than the layers above it; the surgeon switches to scissors, whose blunt tips she slides beneath it to lift it clear of what lies underneath.

Beneath the fascia the muscle is split along its fibres rather than cut across them, because the fibres will knit faster if they are only parted, and the assistant holds the edges apart with a pair of broad retractors; the circulating nurse, who has not yet been spoken to, steps in to adjust the lamp by a hand's breadth.

Now the peritoneum, a membrane thin enough to let the viscera show grey-blue through it, a membrane that must be tented before it is entered; the surgeon lifts a fold of it with forceps, the assistant lifts a second fold a centimetre away, and the scissors go between the two, opening a window that is then extended in both directions with a finger, until the whole wound stands open and the abdomen declares itself.

The organ is found where the imaging promised it would be, bound to its neighbours by adhesions, and these are taken down patiently with the blade's flat edge.

The pedicle is isolated, skeletonised, clamped in two places, and divided between the clamps; the specimen comes free and is passed off the field in a basin, where the pathologist's runner is already waiting.

The surgeon ties the stump twice, first a free tie seated hard against the clamp, then a transfixion stitch beneath it, because a single knot has been known to slip, and the bed is irrigated with warm saline, and the fluid is drawn off, and the field is inspected dry for a full minute.

The count is called and answered aloud: sponges, forty; needles, eleven; blades, three, all present; nothing has been left in a place where it could be forgotten. Then the closure begins, which proceeds in the exact reverse of the opening: peritoneum and posterior sheath together in a continuous absorbable suture, anterior sheath in interrupted bites a centimetre apart, each bite set a centimetre back from the edge, so that the knots lie flat when the ends are cut short and the tissue is not strangled.

The skin is brought together last with a subcuticular line that will leave almost nothing to see.

A dressing is laid over it, squared to the wound, and when the drapes come down the patient is a person again, and the anaesthetist begins to lighten the gas while the monitor keeps its steady green reckoning; the surgeon strips her gloves and writes the operative note standing, which takes her four minutes. The room is turned over for the next case.

The theatre holds its light in a single disciplined column, which falls from the ceiling array onto a rectangle of prepared skin, and because the room has been cooled to a temperature that suits instruments rather than people, the gowned bodies at the table move with a slight deliberate stiffness, and the anaesthetist at the head counts the drip in silence; the first assistant has already draped the field, which narrows the whole patient to one amber window of abdomen, and the surgeon lifts the blade to open it, and the stroke she makes is unhurried, a line that she has rehearsed a thousand times on cadaver and on living tissue, and the skin parts behind the edge as cleanly as paper divides when a weight is allowed to travel down it, so that the subcutaneous fat rises yellow into view before the bleeding begins, before anyone has to reach to stop it, and already the scrub nurse has the gauze in hand.

Beneath the dermis lies the fascia, a pale sheet that must be cut along its fibres, that will not forgive a careless angle, that the second assistant steadies with a pair of toothed forceps in order to keep the tension even; the diathermy sings its brief flat note, the capillaries seal as the current touches them, the smoke lifts and is drawn away by the suction, and the field dries to the colour of wet rope while the counting of swabs continues at the side table in a low voice.

Now the muscle is separated rather than divided, the fibres pushed apart with blunt forceps and then with fingers, and the retractor arms are set and tightened until the opening holds itself wide without a hand on it.

The peritoneum comes up as a glassy membrane, which the surgeon tents between two clamps, and she nicks it with scissors held flat, a small controlled puncture that admits the air and lets the viscera settle away from the blade.

Inside, the bowel lies in its loose coils, which glisten and shift faintly with the ventilator's rhythm, and the surgeon begins to pack them upward with warm damp swabs to clear the lower quadrant before she can reach the inflamed appendix; the registrar names each swab aloud as it goes in, counting them in order to protect the count at the end.

The appendix, when it is delivered into the wound, proves thickened and dusky, a swollen finger that the surgeon lifts gently on the tip of a right-angled clamp, and the mesoappendix that feeds it is stretched into a translucent fan, and she takes the vessel within it between two ties, which the assistant knots down with flat secure throws, and the tissue is then divided between them, so that the organ hangs free on its base alone, and the base is crushed and ligated in turn to be certain of the seal, so that when the specimen is finally cut away above the ligature nothing weeps into the cavity, and the stump sits clean and dark against the caecum.

The specimen goes into a pot to be labelled and sent, and the circulating nurse writes the time on the lid.

The cavity is then washed with warm saline to carry away the contamination; the suction takes it back; the fluid runs clear by the third lavage, and the surgeon inspects the gutters and the pelvic floor, and the packs come out in the order they went in, while the scrub nurse calls the number and receives agreement.

Closure begins from the deepest layer outward: the peritoneum and the posterior sheath are taken together on a round-bodied needle, and the surgeon runs a continuous suture along the line of the wound, while the assistant follows with the forceps, holding the edge forward, keeping the loop from slackening.

The muscle is allowed to fall back into its own plane without stitching; nothing holds it but the layers above and below, and the anterior sheath is approximated next with interrupted absorbable throws, which the surgeon sets a centimetre apart and tests with a finger as she goes; the fat is left alone, which is the usual practice here, which the registrar has been taught to accept without argument, since a buried stitch in fat does nothing but invite infection to find a home, and bleeds besides.

The skin is closed last with a subcuticular line that leaves no ladder of marks.

The surgeon ties the final knot beneath the dermis, where it will dissolve unseen in a matter of weeks, and when the adhesive strip has been laid along the closure and the dressing pressed down at its margins, the anaesthetist begins to lighten the gas that has kept the patient still, and the room's attention turns to the trolley and the transfer, which must be made smoothly; the lamp is swung aside, the count is declared correct and signed, the instruments go down in their trays for the next case.

The theatre, which holds its light in a single disc above the table, falls silent at the moment the anaesthetist lifts two fingers and the monitor settles into a steady green pulse, and the senior surgeon takes the blade from the scrub nurse's gloved palm, a nurse who has counted the instruments twice already, to begin the first incision, and the skin parts along the drawn line, a line that was inked in the anteroom and traced again under the drape, once the field had been painted amber to render the abdomen a map of itself, so that when the knife descends, where the lamp burns hottest, nothing may be left to guess, and the bleeding points declare themselves at once.

The assistant, who stands opposite with the retractor already angled, whose forearms brace against the table's edge, whose whole attention is a kind of stillness, waits to receive the diathermy; the small vessels are sealed one by one as the smoke rises, as the suction clears it, as the room's breathing resumes.

Beneath the fat the fascia shows its pale grain: the surgeon nicks it with the scalpel's tip and runs the scissors along the fibres, while the assistant lifts the edge clear.

The muscle beneath is divided along its seam, a seam that the anatomy has provided rather than the knife; the bellies are drawn apart on either side, which the retractor blades then hold.

The peritoneum rises in a tented fold between two forceps, a fold that the surgeon pinches and the assistant steadies, and is opened with a stroke small enough to admit air before it admits steel; the cavity exhales its warm, faintly sweet breath, which the team has learned not to name aloud.

The lamp is swung lower by the circulating nurse, who leans back to judge the angle, whose hands never cross the sterile line, and the bowel is packed away in moistened swabs, which the assistant counts, which the scrub nurse records on the board, and the gallbladder comes into view, and the surgeon lays a finger on it to test its tension, until the fundus is grasped and lifted toward the diaphragm.

The dissection proceeds along the neck of the organ, to expose the triangle of safety, and the duct is cleared of fat with slow, blunt sweeps.

Two clips are placed on the duct, one proximal and one distal; the artery is identified beside it and clipped likewise, and the duct is divided between them, after the critical view has been confirmed aloud by both surgeons.

The organ is stripped from its bed with the hook: the tissue parts in small white threads, and the liver surface weeps a little, where the current is applied, where the oozing stops, where the bed goes dry and pale.

The specimen is lifted free into a retrieval bag: the bag is closed, the drawstring is pulled, and the whole is drawn through the upper opening, which the assistant widens with a finger, until it passes; the cavity is then washed with warm saline, which is instilled and suctioned twice, which runs clear at the second pass, before the packs are removed and the count is called, to be answered by the scrub nurse, as the circulating nurse repeats the number.

The drain is laid along the bed, a soft tube that exits through a separate stab.

The closure begins from the deep layer outward, a sequence that nobody hurries, while the fascia is run with a looped suture and the fat is approximated loosely, so that the skin, which is drawn together with subcuticular stitch, lies flat, and the dressing is laid on by the nurse, who smooths it with the flat of her hand; the lamp is raised, the drapes come away, the patient is wheeled toward recovery.

The theatre is a white room held at eighteen degrees, which the overhead lamps flood from two angles so that nothing on the field can cast a shadow, and because the table has already been tilted a few degrees head-down, the viscera settle away from the diaphragm and the working space opens of its own accord; the first assistant, a woman who has scrubbed in silence for eleven minutes, now steps up to receive the drapes, and the circulating nurse passes them in the order they will be needed, which the scrub nurse confirms aloud, and the count begins, since every sponge must be recorded before the knife is permitted to touch skin, so that when the closure comes, hours from now, nobody will have to open the abdomen again to find what was lost, and the anaesthetist, meanwhile, notes the baseline.

The surgeon takes the scalpel, a number ten blade seated on a heavy handle, which she has used since her residency, which she will not hand to anyone else before the fascia is open, and draws it once through the skin: the line runs from two fingerbreadths below the xiphoid to the umbilicus, the dermis parts cleanly, the subcutaneous fat separates in a yellow lip along the whole length.

Blood wells into the incision in fine beads, dozens of them at once along both edges; the assistant blots and the diathermy pencil touches each bleeder in turn, until the line has gone quiet and pale.

Beneath the fat lies the linea alba, which the surgeon exposes with the back of the forceps; she scores it, and a dark seam appears along the midline, which she follows upward with the pencil on cutting current.

The peritoneum rises as a grey membrane that balloons slightly with each breath the ventilator delivers, and she lifts it between two clamps to avoid taking bowel with it, then opens it on a scissor-stroke; the assistant slides in a moist lap pad, which keeps the loops of small intestine from presenting themselves at the wound.

The self-retaining retractor, which takes two people to seat properly, is now fixed to the rail that runs along the table's left edge, and its blades are packed with folded gauze, which protects the wound edges, which would otherwise be bruised by eight hours of steady traction; the assistant cranks the arms open by half-turns, and the surgeon watches the colour of the liver edge to be certain that the pressure is tolerable, and the field widens into something she can work in.

The stomach is mobilised first, the surgeon dividing the gastrocolic ligament vessel by vessel, and the assistant holds countertraction with a sponge stick.

Dissection proceeds toward the hilum: the nodes come away in a single packet, the specimen is lifted free and dropped into a basin, and the resident carries it to the door, where the pathology runner is waiting.

Now the reconstruction begins; the surgeon changes gloves, and the scrub nurse lays out the loaded needle drivers in a row, because the anastomosis will take forty minutes of uninterrupted suturing, during which the lamp must not be moved, the suction must not whistle, and the conversation must stop.

The bowel ends are brought together without tension: the posterior layer goes in first, then the anterior, which the surgeon places in interrupted bites a bare three millimetres apart, and the assistant follows each throw with the scissors; the suture line is tested with a gentle pinch of air, which produces no leak, which satisfies her, so that the drain can be sited low in the pelvis, with its tip brought out through a separate stab, and the abdomen declared ready to close.

The final count is called, and it matches the first, which is announced twice for the record.

Closure runs in layers from the deep fascia outward, which the surgeon takes in a continuous looped suture, while the assistant keeps the edges aligned with toothed forceps and the anaesthetist begins lightening the gas, until the patient's breathing returns to a rhythm the machine no longer drives; the skin is apposed with clips that lie flat under the dressing, and the drapes come down. The room exhales.

The theatre is a room of pale tile and colder light, whose six lamps converge upon a single rectangle of draped skin, and because the body beneath has already been counted, weighed, and named aloud, the team moves without hurry; the scrub nurse, who has laid her instruments in the order of their use, begins to pass them one at a time, and the surgeon takes the blade she offers, which rides in her palm handle-first and is received without a word, as the first cut opens the abdomen along a line marked earlier in violet ink, the pressure measured so that the dermis parts cleanly before the fat yields, until the yellow lobules bloom outward and the assistant blots them away.

The incision runs eight inches below the navel, which the resident steadies with two gloved fingers, which do not tremble, which the attending has watched for three months in order to trust them now; the room keeps its own time — the ventilator counts in sixes, the monitor answers in greens, the circulating nurse marks the hour on the board.

Beneath the fat lies the fascia, pearl-white and fibrous: the surgeon scores it with the tip of the blade, then widens the score with scissors while the assistant holds the retractor steady against the pelvic wall.

The muscle bellies are separated rather than divided, which spares the fibres their blood supply; the retractor blades go in at once, and the halves of the rectus, which have never truly been joined, part like a curtain.

Under them waits the peritoneum, a membrane so thin that it lifts in a tent between two forceps and transmits the shadow of the bowel behind it; the surgeon nicks it to admit a finger before she extends the opening with scissors, and the cavity declares itself — a wet, warm, breathing room that the lamps now have to find.

The anaesthetist, who has deepened the agent a half-percent to relax the wall, reports a pressure that holds at ninety-eight, and the attending nods without lifting her eyes; the suction clears a thin serous pool that has gathered in the gutter, and the packs go in, which are counted aloud as they enter, which will be counted again at the end — the resident says eight, the nurse repeats eight, and the figure is written on the board in order to be read back later, when the wound is ready for closing and nothing may remain inside.

Now the segment is found: a loop of ileum thickened to the touch, dusky at its mesenteric edge, and the surgeon runs it between finger and thumb for a hand's breadth on either side.

She calls for the stapler to divide it, the nurse answers with the cartridge, the jaws close and fire with a sound like a stapled page, and the two ends fall apart, bloodless at the staple line, while the assistant lifts the specimen clear.

The mesentery is taken next in small bites — the clamps go on in pairs, the vessels are tied with silk, and the knots are laid flat so that each throw seats down against the last, the first square, the second square, the third a safety.

What remains is to restore continuity: the ends are brought together without tension, and the surgeon lays her posterior row with fine absorbable thread, which she runs in a single line and locks at the corner; she then turns the anastomosis, which must be inspected along its whole circumference, which the resident rotates toward the light so that the attending can test it between two fingers, feeling for a lumen the width of a thumb and finding none of the puckering that would announce a stricture.

The packs come out, and the count is called: eight, eight, correct — the sponges, the needles, the blades, all accounted for.

The cavity is washed with warm saline until the returning fluid runs clear, and because the peritoneum closes itself in time, the surgeon takes only the fascia, running a looped suture from each end toward the middle while the assistant keeps the edges approximated with forceps that do not bruise; the skin is last, stapled or sewn as the tissue allows, the subcuticular line chosen here for a patient who is thirty-one — and then the drape comes down, the lights swing up, the table is unlocked.
